questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in a static array given its index?
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations. Because the memory address of any element can be computed directly using its base address and index offset, access time is constant, or O(1).

questions.questionText: In languages like C and C++, strings are typically represented as arrays of characters terminated by a null character ('\0').
questions.explanation: C-style strings are character arrays conventioned to end with a null terminator byte (\0), which allows functions like strlen() and printf() to know where the string ends.

questions.questionText: What is the primary reason that inserting an element in the middle of a dynamic array has a worst-case time complexity of O(n)?
options: Because you must rehash the entire array
Because elements after the insertion point must be shifted to make space
Because the array must be sorted after insertion
Because strings require dynamic memory reallocation
questions.correctAnswer: Because elements after the insertion point must be shifted to make space
questions.explanation: To maintain contiguous memory and preserve the relative order of elements, inserting an element at an arbitrary index requires shifting all subsequent elements one position to the right, taking linear time O(n).

questions.questionText: Modifying a mutable string in place is always more memory-efficient than creating a new string, regardless of the programming language used.
questions.explanation: Many languages (like Java, Python, and JavaScript) feature immutable strings for security, caching, and thread-safety reasons. While in-place mutation avoids allocating new objects, language semantics and garbage collection overhead dictate overall efficiency.

questions.questionText: Which of the following operations generally requires O(n) time complexity for both standard arrays and typical strings?
options: Finding the length (when not explicitly cached)
Appending an element to a pre-allocated static array
Modifying an element at a known index
questions.correctAnswer: Finding the length (when not explicitly cached)
questions.explanation: In null-terminated strings or arrays where length isn't stored as a metadata attribute, you must traverse the entire structure until the end marker is reached, which takes O(n) time.

questions.questionText: What is the primary structural invariant that distinguishes an AVL tree from a standard Binary Search Tree (BST)?
options: Every node must have exactly two children or be a leaf.
The heights of the left and right subtrees of any node can differ by at most 1.
All leaves must reside at the exact same depth.
The left child must always contain a value greater than the right child.
questions.correctAnswer: The heights of the left and right subtrees of any node can differ by at most 1.
questions.explanation: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST where the difference between heights of left and right subtrees (balance factor) for any node is restricted to the set {-1, 0, 1}.

questions.questionText: True or False: Every valid AVL tree is also a valid Red-Black tree if appropriate node colors (red and black) can be assigned.
questions.explanation: Because AVL trees are more strictly balanced than Red-Black trees (AVL height is bounded by roughly 1.44 log n, whereas Red-Black height is bounded by 2 log n), any AVL tree's structure can be colored to satisfy all Red-Black tree properties.
questions.concept: Comparison of AVL and Red-Black Balances

questions.questionText: In a Red-Black Tree, what color is a newly inserted node typically assigned before any structural fixes or recoloring takes place?
options: It depends on the color of the parent node
questions.explanation: Newly inserted nodes in a Red-Black tree are always colored red initially to avoid violating the black-height property, as inserting a black node would directly change the black-height of paths passing through it.

questions.questionText: Which rotation type is required to fix an 'Right-Left' (RL) imbalance in an AVL tree?
options: Double Right-Left Rotation (Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on parent)
Double Left-Right Rotation (Left rotation on child, then Right rotation on parent)
questions.correctAnswer: Double Right-Left Rotation (Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on parent)
questions.explanation: An RL imbalance occurs when a node's right subtree is too tall, and within that right subtree, the left child is too tall. This requires a right rotation on the right child followed by a left rotation on the unbalanced node.

questions.questionText: True or False: The worst-case time complexity for a search operation in both AVL trees and Red-Black trees of size n is O(log n).
questions.explanation: Both AVL trees and Red-Black trees maintain a strictly bounded height proportional to O(log n), ensuring that search operations take logarithmic time in the worst case.

quizzes.topicName: Graph Representations, Traversals, and Shortest Path Algorithms

questions.questionText: What is the worst-case time complexity of finding all-pairs shortest paths using the Floyd-Warshall algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.explanation: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm utilizes three nested loops running up to V iterations each to consider all possible intermediate vertices for every pair of vertices, resulting in a time complexity of O(V^3) regardless of the number of edges.

questions.questionText: In a sparse graph, an Adjacency List representation is generally more memory-efficient than an Adjacency Matrix.
questions.explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space, which requires significantly less memory than an adjacency matrix's O(V^2) space when the graph is sparse (i.e., E is much less than V^2).

questions.questionText: Which graph traversal algorithm is naturally suited for finding the shortest path (in terms of number of edges) in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores the graph level by level, ensuring that the first time a node is visited, the path taken from the source is the shortest possible in terms of edge count. DFS does not guarantee shortest paths.

questions.questionText: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail or produce incorrect results when the graph contains negative edge weights?
options: It assumes that once a vertex's shortest distance is finalized, it can never be improved by a subsequently processed vertex with a smaller tentative distance.
It requires a directed acyclic graph to function.
It exceeds the maximum recursion depth.
questions.correctAnswer: It assumes that once a vertex's shortest distance is finalized, it can never be improved by a subsequently processed vertex with a smaller tentative distance.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach relies on the property that adding a non-negative edge weight will never decrease the total path distance. Negative edges violate this monotonicity, meaning a finalized vertex could theoretically be reached via a shorter path later.

questions.questionText: When representing a directed graph, the adjacency matrix is always symmetric along its main diagonal.
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix is symmetric only for undirected graphs because an edge from u to v implies an edge from v to u. In directed graphs, a directed edge from u to v (matrix[u][v] = 1) does not guarantee a directed edge from v to u, making the matrix asymmetric.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about the adjacency‑matrix representation of a graph with V vertices is true?
options: It uses O(V) space regardless of the number of edges.
It uses O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges.
It allows O(1) time to iterate over all outgoing edges of a vertex.
It is the most efficient representation for sparse graphs.
questions.correctAnswer: It uses O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges.
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix always stores a V×V boolean or weight entry, so its space consumption is Θ(V²) no matter how many edges exist. Option A is wrong because the space grows quadratically, not linearly. Option C is wrong because iterating over outgoing edges requires scanning an entire row (Θ(V)). Option D is wrong because for sparse graphs an adjacency list (Θ(V+E)) is far more space‑efficient.

questions.questionText: In a BFS traversal of a directed graph, every edge is classified either as a tree edge or a cross edge.
questions.explanation: BFS on a directed graph can produce four edge types: tree, forward, back, and cross edges. The statement omits forward and back edges, making it false. In undirected graphs only tree and cross edges appear, but the question explicitly says "directed".

questions.questionText: Which condition is required for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee correct shortest‑path results?
options: The graph may contain negative edge weights.
All edge weights must be non‑negative.
The algorithm uses a stack to select the next vertex.
It works correctly even if the graph contains a negative‑weight cycle.
questions.correctAnswer: All edge weights must be non‑negative.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy selection assumes that once a vertex is extracted from the priority queue its distance is final, which fails if negative edges exist. Therefore the algorithm requires non‑negative edge weights. Options A and D contradict this requirement, and option C describes DFS, not Dijkstra.

questions.questionText: The Bellman‑Ford algorithm can detect the presence of a negative‑weight cycle reachable from the source.
questions.explanation: After V‑1 relaxation passes, Bellman‑Ford performs one extra pass; if any edge can still be relaxed, a negative‑weight cycle reachable from the source exists. Hence the statement is true.

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of performing a depth‑first search (DFS) on a graph stored as an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: DFS visits each vertex once (Θ(V)) and explores each adjacency list entry once (Θ(E)). Therefore the total running time is Θ(V + E). The other options over‑estimate the work: O(V²) applies to dense adjacency‑matrix traversals, O(E log V) would be for algorithms using a priority queue, and O(V·E) is far too large for DFS.

quizzes.topicName: Linear Data Structures: Arrays, Stacks, and Queues

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by its index in a static, one-dimensional array?
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations. Because the memory address of any element can be computed directly using a base address and index arithmetic, access time is constant, i.e., O(1).

questions.questionText: Which data structure is most appropriate for evaluating arithmetic expressions in Postfix (Reverse Polish) notation?
questions.explanation: A Stack operates on a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) basis, making it ideal for tracking operands and operators in expression evaluation where the most recently seen items need to be processed first.

questions.questionText: In a standard queue implemented using a circular array of fixed capacity $N$, how do you determine if the queue is full (assuming standard pointers 'front' and 'rear')?
questions.explanation: In a circular queue, wrapping around requires modulo arithmetic. The queue is full when the next position of the rear pointer (wrapping around via modulo) equals the front pointer.

questions.questionText: True or False: Standard push and pop operations on a stack implemented with a singly linked list take O(n) time in the worst case.
questions.explanation: When pushing and popping at the head of a singly linked list, both operations take O(1) time because pointer manipulation occurs strictly at one end without needing to traverse the list.

questions.questionText: What is the primary drawback of using a standard (non-circular) linear array to implement a Queue where elements are enqueued at the rear and dequeued from the front?
options: Memory becomes fragmented and unusable even when space is available ('false overflow').
It requires a doubly linked list underneath.
questions.correctAnswer: Memory becomes fragmented and unusable even when space is available ('false overflow').
questions.explanation: As items are dequeued from the front, the front index moves forward, leaving unused space behind. Even if the array is not physically full, the rear pointer will eventually hit the array boundary, creating a false overflow.
